extracted.intended_audience: writers, students, and general readers interested in narratology and narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive taxonomy for narration choices: who tells a story and how (person, tense, viewpoint, and techniques) including examples and effects. Useful for writers and students deciding narrative mode and devices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narration (definition and role)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration is the use of a written or spoken commentary to convey a story to an audience; it is conveyed by a narrator who delivers information about the plot. Narration is a required element of written stories (novels, short stories, poems, memoirs) and optional in some other storytelling formats (films, plays, TV, video games).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish who tells the story and what information the narrator provides; determine whether narration is necessary given the medium (e.g., optional in visual media where action/dialogue can carry the story).

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative mode (set of choices shaping narration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrative mode encompasses the set of choices through which the creator develops their narrator and narration: narrative point of view/perspective/voice (grammatical person and scope of knowledge), narrative tense (past/present/future), and narrative technique (methods like setting, character development, theme exploration, plot structure, selective detail, genre norms, stylistic devices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the above dimensions as interdependent design decisions: pick person, tense and techniques to support desired reader distance, information flow, and tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative point of view (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The choice of grammatical person used by the narrator to establish whether narrator and audience are participants in the story; also includes the scope of information or knowledge the narrator presents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide both the grammatical person and the narrator's epistemic scope (what they know/see) to control reader alignment, suspense, and reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of narrator (anonymous, character, author-as-character)
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrators may be anonymous/unspecified, a character participating in their story, or the author themself as a character; they may relate events without involvement and have varied awareness of characters' thoughts and distant events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose narrator type to affect intimacy and authority — e.g., anonymous narrator can feel impartial, a character-narrator creates immediacy or bias, author-as-character foregrounds fictionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of narrator knowledge / epistemic access
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of information or knowledge the narrator presents (what they can report about events, characters' thoughts, and distant events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use limited scope to create mystery and focus; use broad/omniscient scope to provide context and multiple-character insight. Explicitly decide and consistently signal what the narrator can and cannot know.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Reveals the story through an openly self-referential and participating narrator using first-person pronouns (I, me, we), creating a close relationship between narrator and reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverages intimacy and subjective voice; good for interiority and unreliable narration but limits knowledge to the narrator's experience. Examples: many memoirs and character-focused novels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Narrator recounts experience using the second-person pronoun you; can create distance (often ironic) while appearing to address the reader or an implied addressee. In some interactive/game formats 'you' addresses the player-character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-person can be immersive or distancing depending on framing; common in experimental fiction and gamebooks. Note difference between addressed reader devices and true second-person narration with an implicit narrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration refers to characters with third-person pronouns (he, she, they) and never first- or second-person pronouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Third-person allows flexibility of distance and can be paired with omniscient, limited, subjective or objective techniques. Choose pronoun usage to shape focalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person omniscient
rubrics_metrics.description: A narrator with an overarching perspective who sees and knows everything happening in the story world, including characters' thoughts and feelings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Typical of many 19th-century novels (e.g., Dickens, Tolstoy). Use omniscience to provide broad context and multiple inner lives but beware of flattening immediacy or reader alignment if overused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-person limited / close third
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view confined to one character's perspective; narration follows the thoughts/observations of that focal character without full omniscience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers a balance between first-person intimacy and third-person flexibility. Use close third to access interiority while retaining narrator distance; example: J. M. Coetzee's Disgrace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subjective vs objective point of view
rubrics_metrics.description: Subjective POV conveys the thoughts, feelings and opinions of one or more characters; objective POV tells a story without describing characters' inner states, presenting an unbiased external account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subjective narration supports character psychology and empathy; objective narration can create dramatic irony or require readers to infer motivation from action/dialogue ('show, don't tell').

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternating / multiple narrators and multiperspectivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Using multiple points of view (different narrators, alternating first/third persons, or distinct focal characters in separate sections/chapters) or framing devices (stories within stories) to present varied perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternation can illuminate contrasts between characters, develop complex social identity, or structure large narratives (e.g., Song of Ice and Fire, The English Patient). Use clear signaling to avoid confusing readers; framing can connect disparate tales thematically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planes of point of view (Uspensky): spatial, temporal, psychological, phraseological, ideological
rubrics_metrics.description: Point of view can be expressed on multiple planes: spatial (where attention is placed), temporal (time perspective), psychological (character behavior/inner life), phraseological (linguistic register), and ideological (values/worldview).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider each plane when designing POV: e.g., phraseological choices (register, diction) can reveal narrator or character voice; ideological stance may be explicit or deep-structure and shapes interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Psychological point of view (distance / affinity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Focuses on characters' behaviors and encompasses the narrator's distance or affinity to each character and event represented in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use psychological focalization to control empathy and ironic distance; be mindful that this is complex to formalize and affects reader alignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideological point of view (explicit vs embedded ideology)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator's norms, values, beliefs and worldview; may be stated outright (explicit ideology) or embedded at deep-structural levels (implicit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make ideological stance explicit when you want clear commentary; embed ideology for subtler, interpretive layers. Recognize that analysis of ideology often relies on intuition and close reading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative tense (past, present, future)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tense choice establishes temporal relation of events to narrator's present: past (events occurred before narrator's present; most common), present (events depicted as occurring now; gives immediacy; includes 'historical present'), and future (rare, often prophetic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Past tense is default for many stories; present tense gives immediacy and is common in spoken narratives and some modern novels (e.g., Hunger Games); future tense creates a prophetic tone. Screenplays typically use present tense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream-of-consciousness technique
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique that attempts to replicate a character's thought processes (often first-person), including interior monologues, inner desires, fragmented or incomplete thoughts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use for deep interiority and psychological realism (e.g., Joyce, Faulkner). Balance readability with authenticity; structure may still be needed to maintain reader engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unreliable narrator technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of an untrustworthy narrator to give readers a sense of disbelief or ambiguity about what is true; commonly first-person but can be third-person as well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deploy to generate mystery, irony, or thematic complexity (e.g., Catcher in the Rye). Provide clues that invite readers to question the narrator rather than simply confusing them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrative technique (miscellaneous methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other methods used to narrate a story, including establishing setting, developing characters, exploring themes, structuring plot, intentionally expressing certain details but not others, following or subverting genre norms, employing linguistic styles, and other storytelling devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select techniques that serve the story's aims—e.g., selective detail for focus, genre subversion to surprise readers, stylistic devices (tone, diction) to create voice. Combine techniques coherently with chosen POV and tense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium suitability of narration
rubrics_metrics.description: Narration is optional in many storytelling formats (films, plays, TV, video games) because those media can convey story via dialogue and visual action rather than explicit commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When adapting between media, reassess whether explicit narration is necessary or whether visual/dialogue techniques can substitute; interactive formats (gamebooks, interactive fiction) often use addressed-reader devices.
